1226.title: The Pittsburgh Platform (1885)
1226.hook: early American Reform set aside many rituals
1226.howItsDone: Reform Jews and historians read the Pittsburgh Platform as an early statement of American Reform principles; Reform congregations today often study it alongside later statements of the movement.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Reform Judaism, and the man at the kitchen table who decided the candles stay. Your line: informed choice. Today, an early, bold statement of what Reform would choose.

A room in Pittsburgh. A group of Reform rabbis around a table, papers everywhere, arguing late. They are not writing a prayer or a law code. They are writing a platform: a short list of principles, the way a political party does, saying plainly what their movement holds and what it is ready to let go. The document they finish is blunt enough that people are still quoting it, and still arguing with it. Some readers find it brave. Some find it a loss. Today, you read a few of its lines for yourself.
screen: `A ROOM IN PITTSBURGH.` → `A LIST OF PRINCIPLES.` → `STILL QUOTED, STILL ARGUED WITH.`

segments.voice: The Pittsburgh Platform. Its sentences are long and careful, so take them slowly. First, the law. Speaking of the laws of Moses, the rabbis wrote that "we accept as binding only its moral laws, and maintain only such ceremonies as elevate and sanctify our lives, but reject all such as are not adapted to the views and habits of modern civilization." The moral laws stay binding. Ceremonies stay too, if they lift a life. What goes is what, in their view, no longer fit. Second, the details. The platform named the laws about diet, priestly purity and dress as belonging to another age, and said keeping them could get in the way of spiritual life now. So kosher kitchens and much else were set aside as obligations. Third, the people. "We consider ourselves no longer a nation, but a religious community," it said, expecting no return to the land and no restored sacrificial worship. Fourth, justice. The platform closed by calling it a duty to help solve the problems of society on the basis of justice and righteousness. Hold all four together and you see the shape of early American Reform: ethics and reason in the middle, much of ritual at the edge. Some Jews at the time welcomed it. Others were deeply troubled by it, and the arguments it started helped draw the lines between the movements. Tomorrow, what later Reform did with it.
screen: `MORAL LAWS BINDING, CEREMONIES TESTED.` · `DIET, PURITY, DRESS SET ASIDE.` · `A RELIGIOUS COMMUNITY, NOT A NATION.` · `A DUTY TO JUSTICE.` · then, large: `SUCH CEREMONIES AS ELEVATE AND SANCTIFY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you once said with total confidence, about yourself, your family, or what matters, and hear it in your old voice. Then ask what you'd say about it now: what stayed exactly the same, what you dropped, what you might want back. Don't scold the old voice; it was doing its best with what it knew.
The Pittsburgh Platform. An early statement of American Reform that kept the moral laws binding, set many rituals aside, and called for justice in society. Today's word.
Your line: the early platform. Bold, blunt, and still argued over today. See you tomorrow.

1227.title: Returning to ritual
1227.hook: later Reform statements embrace more Hebrew and ritual
1227.howItsDone: In Reform congregations today, members may study Hebrew, wear a kippah or prayer shawl if they choose, chant from the Torah and keep Shabbat or holiday rituals, as informed choices rather than obligations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the early platform: moral laws binding, ceremonies tested, much of ritual set aside. Today, what came after.

Two photographs from the same Reform temple, taken a few generations apart. In the older one, a grandfather sits in a dark suit, bareheaded, with an English prayer book. The choir is up front; the rabbi's sermon is the center of the morning. In the newer one, his granddaughter stands at the reading table, a prayer shawl over her shoulders and a kippah pinned in her hair, chanting from the Torah scroll in Hebrew. Same building. Same movement. Nobody forced her. She chose it. Today, how Reform came to make room for that second photograph.
screen: `TWO PHOTOGRAPHS, ONE TEMPLE.` → `BAREHEADED, AN ENGLISH BOOK.` → `A PRAYER SHAWL, HEBREW CHANT.`

segments.voice: Returning to ritual. Reform did not stop at its early platform. Its rabbis kept writing new statements of principles, and later ones, including one adopted, as it happens, in Pittsburgh again, sound different from the first. Take it in three moves. First, Hebrew. The later statement encourages Reform Jews to study Hebrew, the language of the Torah and the prayer book, so they can meet the texts for themselves. Second, the commandments. Where the early platform set many rituals aside, the later one calls for ongoing study of the whole range of mitzvot, the commandments, and for taking on those that speak to a person and a community. Shabbat, the holy days, prayer, even the dietary laws are back on the table, not as rules handed down, but as invitations. Third, what did not change. This is still informed choice, with ethics at the center. The return is chosen, not required. An old line fits it. At Sinai, the people answered Moses: "All that the LORD hath said will we do, and be obedient." In Hebrew, the order is do, then hear. The Talmud tells of a heavenly voice that praised Israel for putting the doing first. Some Reform Jews describe their own return that way: light the candles first, and the meaning comes after. The granddaughter is not going back to her grandfather's world, or to anyone else's. She is returning, on her own terms, to something the family once set down.

1228.title: Prophetic Judaism
1228.hook: Reform places the prophets' call for justice at the center
1228.howItsDone: Reform congregations organize social action, such as feeding programs and advocacy, as central religious work, and quote prophets like Amos and Isaiah in sermons and statements of principle.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: returning. The granddaughter at the reading table, choosing a ritual her family once set down. Today, the part of Reform that never left.

"Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free." That line is read aloud on Yom Kippur morning, to a room full of people who have not eaten since the night before. Stomachs are empty. Some heads ache. And the reading, from the prophet Isaiah, turns around and asks them what the fast is for. Not the hunger alone, it says. The hungry person down the street. Today, a movement that takes that question as its center.
screen: `IS NOT THIS THE FAST?` → `A HUNGRY ROOM ON YOM KIPPUR.` → `WHAT IS THE FAST FOR?`

segments.voice: Prophetic Judaism. It is a name Reform Jews use for something at the heart of their movement: the conviction that the prophets' call for justice is the core of Judaism. Three steps. First, the voices. The Hebrew prophets spoke to kings and crowds about how the poor, the widow and the stranger were treated. Amos put it in one picture: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." Not a trickle on holidays; a river that doesn't stop. Isaiah gave a to-do list: "Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow." Second, the thread in Reform. The early platform closed with a duty to help solve society's problems on the basis of justice and righteousness, and that thread runs through the later statements too. Reform congregations organize around it: feeding programs, advocacy, sermons that sound like Amos. When ritual returned, this did not move aside. Third, a fair word. The prophets are not Reform's alone. Their books belong to the Bible that all the streams read, that Yom Kippur reading is heard across the movements, and Jews in each stream give charity and work for justice. What Reform does is put the prophets' call at the very center, and measure ritual by whether it serves it. The prophets were not against prayer or fasting. Isaiah was against fasting that left the oppressed still bound. That is what prophetic means here: faith that has to show up somewhere outside the sanctuary.

1229.title: Progressive Judaism worldwide
1229.hook: Liberal and Progressive movements in Britain, Europe, Israel and beyond
1229.howItsDone: Progressive Jews around the world belong to congregations called Reform, Liberal or Progressive, linked through an international union; they pray in Hebrew and local languages and share commitments to ethics, informed choice and equality.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was prophetic: justice running down like waters, and a fast that turns outward. Today, Reform's family beyond America.

Three signs on three synagogue doors. One, in London, says Liberal. One, in Tel Aviv, says Progressive, in Hebrew. One, in an American suburb, says Reform. Step through any of them on a Friday night and some things will feel familiar: Hebrew and the local language side by side, women and men leading together, a sermon that might quote Amos. Some will feel different: the tunes, the accents, how much Hebrew, what's for dinner after. Three names on three doors. Are they three movements, or one? Today's answer is a little of both.
screen: `LIBERAL, PROGRESSIVE, REFORM.` → `FAMILIAR AND DIFFERENT.` → `THREE MOVEMENTS, OR ONE?`

segments.voice: Progressive Judaism worldwide. Progressive is the family name. In different countries the family members have different first names, and they are linked through an international union of Progressive congregations. Three stops. First, Britain. Two movements grew up there side by side, one called Reform and one called Liberal. Liberal Judaism in Britain grew partly through the work of Lily Montagu, who helped found it and led services herself. The two, each with its own prayer books and rabbis, have been drawing closer under the Progressive name. Second, Europe. On the continent, some congregations call themselves Liberal and some Progressive, and they pray in Hebrew and in their own languages, from Paris to Berlin to Amsterdam. Third, Israel. There the movement calls itself Progressive Judaism, in Hebrew yahadut mitkademet. Its congregations pray in Hebrew as a matter of course, so the question of how much Hebrew simply disappears. Like Masorti communities, they build their life alongside an official rabbinate that is Orthodox. What do the doors share? The ideas from this week: ethics at the center, informed choice, women and men as equals, and the prophets' call. And a verse some of these communities like to quote, from Isaiah: "for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people." Each country has its own door, and its own name on it. The house behind the doors is shared.
screen: `ONE FAMILY, MANY NAMES.` · `BRITAIN: REFORM AND LIBERAL.` · `EUROPE: HEBREW AND LOCAL LANGUAGES.` · `ISRAEL: YAHADUT MITKADEMET.` · then, large: `AN HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL PEOPLE.`

1230.title: Reconstructionist Judaism
1230.hook: Mordecai Kaplan described Judaism as an evolving religious civilization
1230.howItsDone: Reconstructionist Jews, following Mordecai Kaplan, treat Judaism as the evolving civilization of the Jewish people, so congregations embrace Jewish culture, language, history and arts alongside prayer and ritual.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: worldwide. Reform, Liberal, Progressive: one family, many names on many doors. Today, a movement with one big idea in its name.

One shelf in a family's living room. A prayer book with a cracked spine. A cookbook with honey cake stains on the page for the new year. A record of old Yiddish songs. A Hebrew newspaper someone brought back from a trip. A history of the family's town that no longer exists. A pair of Shabbat candlesticks. Which of these things is Judaism? Only the prayer book? Or the whole shelf? A teacher named Mordecai Kaplan gave an answer that started a movement.
screen: `ONE SHELF.` → `PRAYERS, RECIPES, SONGS, HISTORY.` → `WHICH OF THESE IS JUDAISM?`

segments.voice: Reconstructionist Judaism. Kaplan was a rabbi and a teacher, and his answer was: the whole shelf. Judaism, he wrote, is not only a religion, a set of beliefs and rituals. It is a civilization: the whole life of a people, including its language, its land, its history, its literature, its art and music, its food, its customs and its law. Religion is at its heart, he said, but it is not the whole of it. Three words carry the idea. First, civilization. If Judaism is a civilization, then a Jew who sings the songs, studies the history, speaks Hebrew or cooks the holiday foods is taking part in Jewish life, not standing outside it. Second, evolving. Civilizations change; they borrow, adapt and grow. Kaplan argued that Judaism always has, and has to keep doing it to stay alive. That is where the name comes from: each generation reconstructs the tradition for its own time, the way you might rebuild an old house, keeping the foundation and changing the rooms. Third, the people. Kaplan put the Jewish people at the center, the community that carries the civilization forward. A psalm pictures that handing-on: "One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts." Each one receives, and each one builds. Kaplan taught within the Conservative world for a long time, and Reconstructionism grew from his ideas into a movement of its own.
screen: `NOT ONLY A RELIGION.` · `A CIVILIZATION: THE WHOLE SHELF.` · `EVOLVING: EACH GENERATION REBUILDS.` · `THE PEOPLE AT THE CENTER.` · then, large: `ONE GENERATION TO ANOTHER.`

Then, if you like, turn to your own life. What would be on your shelf, and which things there carry a whole civilization?

1231.title: Deciding together
1231.hook: Reconstructionist communities decide their practice together
1231.howItsDone: Reconstructionist congregations decide questions of practice through study and discussion: the rabbi teaches the tradition, members name the values at stake, and the community reaches and records a decision together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Reconstructionist Judaism, and the whole shelf: prayer book, recipes, songs, history. Your line: an evolving civilization. Today, who does the changing.

Tuesday night, a synagogue social hall. Folding chairs in a circle, a coffee urn ticking in the corner, name tags and photocopied pages of text. The question on the table is the kitchen: what food can be served at this congregation's events, and why. Some members keep kosher at home; some don't. One is vegetarian, one has a kid with allergies, one grew up in a home where the kitchen was the center of Jewish life. The rabbi is in the circle, not at a podium. Nobody is going to announce the answer from the front. Tonight, they work it out.
screen: `FOLDING CHAIRS IN A CIRCLE.` → `A QUESTION ABOUT THE KITCHEN.` → `THE RABBI IN THE CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: Deciding together. If Judaism is the evolving civilization of a whole people, as Kaplan taught, a fair question follows: who decides how it evolves? The Reconstructionist answer: the community, together, in three steps. First, study. The rabbi teaches what the Torah, the Talmud and the codes say about the question, so everyone in the circle knows what the past actually says. Kaplan is remembered for saying the past should have a vote, but not a veto. It gets a real voice in the room. Second, values. People name what they care about most here, holiness, welcome, care for animals, care for each other, connection to Jews everywhere, and they listen to each other. Third, the decision. The community decides together what it will do, and writes down why, so the next generation can reconsider it. The rabbi is teacher and guide, a voice in the circle, not the final ruler. This is one way of holding authority, and the other movements hold it in their own ways: you met the Orthodox rabbi who rules from inside the law, and the Conservative mara d'atra who chooses among approved answers. Reconstructionists place more of the deciding in the room. Behind it is an old teaching from Hillel in the Mishnah: do not separate yourself from the community. And a line from Ecclesiastes: "Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour."

1232.title: Kaplan's God
1232.hook: Kaplan pictured God as the power in the world that makes for goodness and fulfillment
1232.howItsDone: Reconstructionist prayer books and teachers often invite worshippers to bring their own understanding of God to prayer, and Kaplan's idea of God as the power that makes for goodness is one of the views discussed in the movement.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: decide together, a community talking a practice through and choosing it as a group. Today, the week closes with God.

On a refrigerator door, a child's crayon drawing: a giant in the clouds with a long white beard, over a small house with a crooked chimney. Ask the artist who that is, and the answer comes fast. God. Some grown-ups still carry that drawing inside them, never revised. Mordecai Kaplan, the thinker behind the Reconstructionist movement, asked a different question: not where God lives, or what God looks like, but what God does in a human life. His answer is today's word.
screen: `A CRAYON GOD ON THE FRIDGE.` → `NEVER REVISED.` → `WHAT DOES GOD DO?`

segments.voice: Kaplan's God. The Torah forbids carving an image of God. You met the name from the burning bush on day eighty-two. In the King James words it is "I AM THAT I AM," and some readers hear the Hebrew as I will be what I will be, a name that won't sit still for a portrait. Maimonides taught that one can say only what God is not, because every positive description falls short. Kabbalists spoke of Ein Sof, the without-end. So Kaplan stepped into an old conversation; he did not start it. He set aside the idea of a God who reaches in from outside nature to work miracles. He described God as the power in the world that makes for salvation, and by salvation he meant goodness and fulfillment in this life: the pull toward honesty, the force that lets a wounded thing heal, the energy that moves people to build fairer lives together. On this view you meet God less as a voice from the sky and more when people take up Micah's charge "to do justly, and to love mercy." Believing in God, for Kaplan, meant trusting that the world holds that power, and joining it. Some readers found his picture freeing, a way to keep praying with honest words. Others, in several movements, replied that a power is not someone who hears, and a prayer needs a listener. Reconstructionist Jews today hold a range of views, and not all follow Kaplan here. His idea leaves a question, not a verdict: what does a picture of God do in the life of the one who holds it?
screen: `NO CARVED IMAGE. I AM THAT I AM.` · `ONLY WHAT GOD IS NOT.` · `THE POWER THAT MAKES FOR GOODNESS.` · `FREEING TO SOME, TOO THIN TO OTHERS.` · then, large: `MANY WAYS TO PICTURE GOD.`

segments.voice: Let the word God come to mind, and see what arrives with it: a face, a light, an empty space, a warmth, a doubt, or nothing at all. Just notice it, and ask where that picture came from. If you pray, you can pray in silence to God as you understand God; if you don't, let the picture be there for a while, then let it go.
Kaplan's God. The power in the world that makes for goodness and fulfillment: one picture of God among several in Jewish thought. Today's word.
Your line: many ways to picture God. Kaplan's is one, in a very old conversation. Another week, complete.
